messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: rebasing feature branches
parts:
I think we should make rebasing optional, but

1. we should encourage users to make commits which don't break
the unit tests, but

2. we'll only enforce that users make merge requests that don't break
unit tests.

I'm a little uncomfortable asking people to blow away their
commit history by rebasing. (There's no getting it back after
a rebase unless you make a duplicate copy, right?)

I'm pretty sure we'll mostly be backing out whole feature branch
merges if we have to back out anything. After all, that's all we'd
be able to do with rebasing. My guess is that we're only going to
be backing things out soon after they are created. Later on, it'll
probably be easier just to patch over them than do surgery on the
commit chain.

As usual, I may be misunderstanding something here or there may
be trouble lurking where I don't expect it, so discussion's more
than welcome.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] rebasing feature branches
parts:
That's roughly my take on things as well Bob.

While I agree that we should try to keep the commit history clean so
that (hopefully) all commits build and pass the unit tests, I think
forcing people to always rewrite their history to a single commit is
too much. Isn't part of the point of something like git over sending
patches around the fact that we can keep the development history of
our contributions?

On top of that, I like to see things nicely split up so that the
development process is not such a mystery. Plus sometimes commits
will come from multiple people (e.g., one person implements, others
doc and unit test), I see no reason to squash those down.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Monday, May 20, 2013 5:15:26 PM UTC-4, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
That's roughly my take on things as well Bob.

While I agree that we should try to keep the commit history clean so
that (hopefully) all commits build and pass the unit tests, I think
forcing people to always rewrite their history to a single commit is
too much.

I don't think anyone is arguing in favor of always rebasing a branch to one commit. It is a question of whether to merge a branch that has

commit A: implement a feature
commit B: implement said feature correctly
maybe more commits

or whether to force a squash of that history to commit AB and maybe more commits.

Isn't part of the point of something like git over sending
patches around the fact that we can keep the development history of
our contributions?
Which history is sought in the above example, with A and B separate or together?

On top of that, I like to see things nicely split up so that the
development process is not such a mystery.  Plus sometimes commits
will come from multiple people (e.g., one person implements, others
doc and unit test), I see no reason to squash those down.

The main reasons to squash doc and unit tests into implementation is that it is easier to understand the rationale for the implementation and to take out all three if the implementation gets reverted. I guess if you squash patches that someone else wrote, it would be reasonable to make the other person the author and you as the committer in the final version.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: rebasing feature branches
parts:
On Monday, May 20, 2013 5:05:42 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I think we should make rebasing optional, but

   1.  we should encourage users to make commits which don't break
       the unit tests, but

   2.  we'll only enforce that users make merge requests that don't break
       unit tests.

That is using git as if it were SVN or CVS. And if commit discipline is voluntary, it won't happen in part because it is extra work and in part because it doesn't do much good for one person to have commit discipline in a project without commit discipline. The guidelines for the Linux kernel

http://www.linuxfoundation.org/content/53-patch-preparation

are pretty good and largely informed by the people who developed git from the outset.

I continue to think that under the old workflow bad pushes were more a symptom of deeper problems than a major problem in their own right. The deeper problems are

-- Bad commits
-- A test suite that has outgrown the capacity of regular laptops to be run often
-- Platform / toolchain / etc. differences

If magically those three problems went away, then pushes / pulls would be a breeze. It looks like we're going to be able to use Hotfoot for testing soon but that is only a partial solution.

I'm a little uncomfortable asking people to blow away their
commit history by rebasing.  (There's no getting it back after
a rebase unless you make a duplicate copy, right?)
I see it more as replacing bad history with good history. Why would you want the bad history back?

I'm pretty sure we'll mostly be backing out whole feature branch
merges if we have to back out anything.  After all, that's all we'd
be able to do with rebasing.  My guess is that we're only going to
be backing things out soon after they are created.  Later on, it'll
probably be easier just to patch over them than do surgery on the
commit chain.

Under SVN / CVS, you rarely revert anything and just add more fixes to the trunk. In the Linux kernel, they revert stuff all the time. Reverting a whole branch is viable but can be a blunt instrument if the branch contains some commits that are good on their own. But you don't really know how long it is going to take before the problem becomes apparent, particularly if you don't have commit discipline so that you don't realize some commit is messed up until a git bisect trips over it.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: rebasing feature branches
parts:
On Tuesday, May 21, 2013 3:39:38 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Could you put these comments into the form of
a recommended practice for developers TODAY?

Today, I don't think it is feasible to do very much. We don't have the machine capacity to test every commit in a pull request; it takes > 10 hours to test the whole pull request (just) on Windows. A human reviewer should at least scan the commit messages and the diffs, and if there is a message like "oops, fix build failure on the previous commit", the human reviewer could say, why don't you rebase this and resubmit the pull request? But if the person submitting the pull request were inclined to rebase, he would have already done so.

It is reasonably simple to do

make clean-all
rebase -i -cmd "make -j8 test-all" HEAD~7

which will run make test-all (or test-unit or whatever) on each of the last 7 + 1 commits. In principle, if you only do make clean-all once at the outset, make should only recompile the affected files on each commit (after the first make -j8 test-all). So, in principle, that should only take about 110% of the time that one make clean-all && make -j8 test-all would take.

In practice, that doesn't work very well. The function_signature*.stan tests generate new function_signature*.cpp files from stanc which thus have a timestamp that is later than the function_signature*.exe binaries, so make will rebake those. Same for test-distributions and for test-models. And for reasons I don't quite understand, make also feels the need to rebake the dependencies of these tests (i.e. bin/stanc.exe). So, the incremental run of make -j8 test-all only omits recompiling bin/libstan.a (which only takes about 5 seconds anyway) and the *_test.cpp files under stan/test/ (which do take a few minutes).

Also, I don't think the test box that Jenkins runs on can do -j8 without swapping, so it does -j4 last I checked. But there are only a couple of places in test-all with extreme RAM spikes (the 2000 line function_signature*.stan tests and bin/stanc), so you end up running the whole test-all with fewer (virtual) cores just to avoid grinding to a halt at a couple of places. With a i7 processor, -j8 isn't twice as fast as -j4 but it's a bit faster on my laptop (where I can do -j8 without swapping as long as I use clang++, O=0, and shuffling).

These problems can be mitigated a lot if you instead utilize ccache ( https://ccache.samba.org/ ) and call the cmd "make -j8 CC='ccache clang++' test-all" iff you first set

export CCACHE_SLOPPINESS=include_file_mtime

which omits the check for the last modification time when comparing the hash of a .cpp file to the hashes of the .cpp files in its cache that it has already compiled. So, make test-all can regenerate a bunch of .cpp files with later timestamps but identical content so that you get a ccache hit.

But there are two problems with ccache. First, it is essentially not available for Windows (it can be used in a full cygwin environment but that doesn't help us much). Second, Stan's practice of utilizing meta-headers such as model_header.hpp and all the src/stan/*.hpp files implies that if any .hpp file in any subdirectory under stan/src/ gets changed, one or more meta-headers will change, and any .cpp file that #includes the changed meta-header will cause a ccache miss even if the .cpp file in question is not actually using the .hpp file that got changed. In other words, if you change just about any header, that will affect model_header.hpp, and cause every .cpp file generated by stanc in test-all to get recompiled even if the resulting optimized binary is identical to what it was before (i.e. the change to the original header doesn't alter the source after the optimization gets rid of the unused code).

So, it isn't really feasible to require pull requests to satisfy test-all at every commit or to require the submitter to first verify on the honor system that test-all is satisfied at every commit. And even if it were, that would just be at O=0 and 1 or 2 platforms. And I don't think saying that people should make their best effort to ensure their commits are good will have much effect because that failed miserably under the old workflow.

Perhaps with a transition plan for where you'd like
us to get to in the FUTURE?

1) Have me pull request the feature/test-headers branch so that we can git rid of src/test/file_includes/ . This actually creates more work for test-all but it makes less work for test-unit. Thus, an individual developer can easily verify that the affected .hpp files precompile by doing make CC=clang++ foo.pch and can do test-unit more often.

2) Split the function_signatures*.stan tests out of test-unit and into test-signatures and include test-signatures in test-all. This will have much the same effect as 1) but I believe will make it possible to eliminate the dependency of test-unit on bin/stanc. Thus, test-unit can be done more often, with more cores, and allow the developer to verify the individual function_signatures tests for the distributions affected by his patch(es), if any.

3) Allow the tests conducted by test-distributions to be conducted individually with a make target. Do this often when you know your changes are affecting a particular distribution.

4) Split a test-grad make target out of test-models that just compiles the models, runs them with --test-grad, and returns 0 iff the lp__ is finite and the AD gradient is close enough to the numerical gradient. Include test-grad in test-all but do test-grad more often than test-models. It is somewhat important to occasionally run a model for a lot of iterations to see if it crashes, but otherwise there is currently too much variability in how the samplers perform to get anything definitive as to whether the model is working or not.

5) Get a Windows server with more capacity than the box Jenkins runs on and put it on Amazon EC2 or something where individual developers can test stuff on Windows before submitting a pull request.

6) Get Hotfoot set up for testing. This is actually close to happening. However, we have to get to the point where each individual test conducted by test-all consumes less than 2GB of RAM because the primary Hotfoot server has a 2GB of RAM per core limitation. With clang++, ccache, and all those cores each doing an individual test, I think we could do (the equivalent of) a make test-all in about 5 minutes.

7) Enable --std=c++11 on Hotfoot so that Stan is C++11 compliant even if it is not using any new C++11 features. This should reduce undefined behaviors, so have people verify that their stuff works on Hotfoot (linux) before testing on the quirkier cases of Windows or Mac llvm-g++-4.2. To get there, we only have to fix two parser bugs (scary warnings about the precedence of >> vs > when overloaded and the implicit template instantiation errors in ast.hpp)

8) Get rid of model_header.hpp and replace it with a lookup table that matches functions used by a particular model to the headers where they are defined. Maybe do something similar with the other meta-headers. Utilize ccache on everything that is not Windows.

9) Then get strict about every commit.

10 World domination.

Ben

Sorry I haven't documented the distributions tests. I'm starting to do that on our wiki. For now, here's how to test a single cauchy test.


First off, the file src/test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_test.hpp is parse by a program in src/test/agrad/distributions/generate_tests.cpp. This program then generates individual unit test files that really stresses the distribution. To generate all the cauchy tests and run the first one:

  make test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00000_generated

The target is the executable test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00000_generated. This looks for a *.o file in the same location. We have written a target for test/*.o to search for a src/test/*_test.cpp file. In this case, it wants to find a src/test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00000_generated.cpp. This hasn't been generated yet, but we've written a specific target in our make/tests, line 53, that depends on the generate_tests executable and the cauchy_test.hpp. It then passes the cauchy_test.hpp file through the executable, which generates a number of cauchy_generated_*****_test.cpp.

For cauchy, 6 tests are generated. You can then run:
  make test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00000_generated
  make test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00001_generated
  make test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00002_generated
  make test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00003_generated
  make test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00004_generated
  make test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00005_generated

To do a 5 minute test-all on Hotfoot we really just need a different set of scripts rather than a Hotfoot make target or a revised set of make targets. I've got it all planned out. The best way to think about Hotfoots batch1 queue is an internet cafe with 256 single core machines each with 2GB of RAM but networked. In this situation, we need a script that calls make hundreds of times.

You can think of the batch4 queue as like a single computer with 12 cores and 16 GB of RAM as you need. There you could just do make -j12 test-all and it would be done in an hour or two iff 12 cores and 16 GB of RAM are available. If not, you have to wait up to 3 days for the job to even start.

If you want to make test-unit do everything except test-distributions and test-models, I guess that is fine. But we would be better served with more granularity. I think we need:

test-headers # will put in pull request tomorrow
test-libstan # basically all the *_test.cpp files under src/test/ excluding src/test/models; avoid dependency on bin/stanc
test-stanc  # all the stuff under src/test/gm
test-distributions # but with subtargets such as test-distribution-cauchy
test-grad # compile all the models and run with --test-grad, check that output is sensible
test-models # depends on test-grad and runs a lot of iterations of each model but doesn't check gradients

Then have test-unit be {test-headers, test-libstan, test-stanc, test-grad} and test-all be {test-unit, test-distributions, test-models}.

Ben

Good question. Yes, there is a programmatic way of determining it, but it's determined by the annotation in the cauchy_test.hpp file. This is the line that gives us that information:
   // Arguments: Doubles, Doubles, Doubles

Here, we have 3 vectorized double arguments. This line indicates that each of the three parameters can be one of these 8 types:
1. double
2. std::vector<double>
3. Eigen::Matrix<double, Eigen::Dynamic, 1>
4. Eigen::Matrix<double, 1, Eigen::Dynamic>
5. var
6. std::vector<var>
7. Eigen::Matrix<var, Eigen::Dynamic, 1>
8. Eigen::Matrix<var, 1, Eigen::Dynamic>

That's 8^3 = 512 tests. I broke the tests into groups of 100. (I tried not breaking up the tests, but unfortunately, Windows craps out.) So for cauchy, this creates 6 tests.

parts:
On Wednesday, May 22, 2013 10:06:13 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
The latter would be best I think. That way, their number can simply be counted rather than trying to predict it. And counting would work even if we change the batch size ever.

Yeah, that's definitely do-able. That was how the tests were originally set up. I split it out into two steps because it was taking too long. Just so you're aware, if you generate all the test cpp files, they get picked up by test-unit.

Can you spec out what you're envisioning? What exactly do you want to type? And what should it generate?

In general, I think anybody should be able to type make test-distribution-cauchy to build and run all the cauchy tests. But that is a bit removed from what I was actually trying to do today, which was move forward with Hotfoot. Here is the body of a test.sh script

cd ${STAN_HOME}
TEST=${TEST_ARRAY[${PBS_ARRAYID}]}
OUT=${TEST//"/"/"-"}
/usr/bin/time --output=${OUTPUT}/${PBS_JOBNAME}_timings.txt --append -f "%C: %E" \
make CC=${CC} ${TEST} > ${OUT}.txt 2> ${OUT}.txt

where

TEST_ARRAY is a large array of individual make targets
PBS_ARRAYID is a counter whose maximum is the number of cores

so basically, for the unit tests, it calls something like

make CC=clang++ test/prob/transform_test.cpp > test-prob-transform_test.txt 2> test-prob-transform_test.txt

and stdout and stderr get redirected to different directories so it is okay that they have the same filename. And the script writes the walltime to a line of a file.

So, we have to build up big arrays of individual make targets. For the distributions tests, this can be accomplished in a somewhat complicated fashion with

unset TEST_ARRAY i
while IFS= read -r -d $'\0' file; do
    TEST=${file/"src/stan/prob"/"test/agrad"}
    TEST=${TEST/".hpp"/""}
    TEST_FILE=src/${TEST}_test.hpp
    if [ ! -e  $TEST_FILE ]
      then continue
    fi
    ARGS=`grep "^// Arguments:" ${TEST_FILE} | sed 's@// Arguments: @@' | wc -w`
    let "N_BATCHES=$[(8 ** $ARGS) / 100]"
    for ((j=0;j<=N_BATCHES;j++)); do
      NUM=`printf "_%05d_generated" ${j}`
      TEST_ARRAY[i++]=${TEST}${NUM}
    done
done < <(find src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/ -type f -name "*.hpp" -print0)

So that looks under src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/ for all the .hpp files, finds the corresponding _test.hpp file, finds the number of trailing words in its "// Arguments:" line, calculates the number of batches of tests, and then appends something like test/agrad/prob/distributions/cauchy_XXXXX_generated to the TEST_ARRAY. And I discovered that was wrong for trunc_normal because it should be 2^5 instead of 8^5.

If there were a step where we could just make all the foo_XXXXX_generated.cpp files for all distributions, then this could basically just be find all the *_generated.cpp files under test/agrad/prob/distributions/univariate and stick them into TEST_ARRAY after chopping off the .cpp.

Ben

7) Enable --std=c++11 on Hotfoot so that Stan is C++11 compliant even if it is not using any new C++11 features. This should reduce undefined behaviors, so have people verify that their stuff works on Hotfoot (linux) before testing on the quirkier cases of Windows or Mac llvm-g++-4.2. To get there, we only have to fix two parser bugs (scary warnings about the precedence of >> vs > when overloaded and the implicit template instantiation errors in ast.hpp)

I can avoid the implicit template instantiation errors in ast.hpp just by adding #include <string>. That results in test-unit passing (with warnings about the precedence of >> vs > still), although I don't know if that was the best fix.

Ben
